principle: Namespace qualification that the enclosing scope already supplies — a prefix on a name, or an `open` of a namespace already open — is not repeated.
A `Decidable` instance is implemented by a computation of the lowest available complexity rather than by transcribing the proposition's definition.
A lemma that rewrites an expression to a strictly simpler normal form is tagged `@[simp]`.
When the core of a proof or construction is a fact about a more general object, it is stated on its own at that general level and the specific result is derived from it.
A goal that a standard finishing tactic (`simp`, `rfl`, `ring`, `grind`, `grw`, `trivial`) closes is closed by that tactic, not by a hand-assembled term or rewrite chain.
A one-argument lambda that only passes its argument to a function is written with the `·` placeholder rather than a named binder.
Declarations added to a file use the variables the file already declares rather than introducing duplicate copies of them.
A notion the library already defines (a predicate, a combinator, a structure) is used by name rather than re-encoded ad hoc in the statement or definition.
A new definition or instance comes with the lemmas that rewrite its applications (`_apply`, `coe_`), so downstream proofs never unfold it.
A structure or class instance is written with `where` syntax rather than an anonymous constructor or record braces.
A definition or theorem stated for a special case is generalised to the parameter it depends on when the special case is recovered by instantiation.
A result the existing library already provides (possibly after exhibiting the object as an instance of the relevant structure) is derived from that API rather than proved again from first principles.
Consecutive top-level commands (`namespace`, `variable`, declarations) are separated by exactly one blank line, never two.
A local `have` or `let` with a short body and few uses is inlined at its use rather than bound to a name.
A terminal `simp` or `simpa` call uses the default simp set with extra lemmas as needed rather than `simp only` with an explicit list.
A structure that extends another is defined directly with all its fields, not in two stages through a named instance of the parent structure.
A `simp` or `grind` call does not list lemmas that are already in the tactic's default set or that it does not need.
An annotation that elaboration supplies on its own — an explicit coercion function, a type ascription, an argument that can be inferred or left to `..` — is not written out.
Consecutive proof steps that a single tactic call can perform (two `simp`s, a `rw` then a `simp`, a `specialize` then a `convert`) are merged into one call.
A declaration's name is built from the constants that actually appear in its statement, following the naming convention.
An instance-implicit argument is left unnamed and recovered with `‹_›` or by inference rather than bound to a name.
A construction that could conflict with a non-definitionally-equal instance on the same type is declared as a `def`, not an `instance`.
A collection of lemmas repeatedly supplied to `simp` locally is registered as a named simp set or tagged `@[simp]` rather than listed with `attribute [local simp]` or in each call.
A lemma whose dual (opposite category, left/right, additive/multiplicative) holds is stated together with that dual.
A non-terminal `simp` is squeezed to `simp only` only when the following tactic depends on the exact goal shape; before a flexible tactic it is left as is.
An automation call (`grind`, `aesop`, `simp`) replaces an explicit proof only when it is not slower and no short readable explicit proof exists.
A module docstring's title names precisely what the file contains, not a broader topic it might suggest.
A definition is an `abbrev` only when it must be reducible for typeclass inference or definitional unfolding; otherwise it is a `def`.
A docstring describes exactly the statement it documents, with the same hypotheses and objects, not a simplified paraphrase or a bare title.
A commonly needed variant or special case of a lemma is stated as its own lemma alongside it.
A docstring is a standalone explanation of its declaration, not a contrast with another declaration.
An import, `open`, `variable`, `section` or section modifier (`noncomputable section`) that another already provides, or that nothing in the file uses or needs, is removed.
A field or projection is named after the library's established name for the same role in analogous structures (`fst`/`snd` for product projections, `inl`/`inr` for coproduct injections).
A multi-line declaration header breaks between the binders and the statement, keeping the conclusion on one line where it fits, rather than splitting it mid-expression.
A constant whose namespace the expected type determines is written with leading-dot notation rather than fully qualified.
Two lemmas each giving half of a conclusion are replaced by one lemma with the combined stronger conclusion.
A lemma about a literal constant (`0`, `1`, `⊤`) whose carrier type cannot be inferred from other arguments takes the type as an explicit argument.
A declaration in a namespace whose short name would shadow a commonly used root-level name (`zero`, `one`, `map`) is marked `protected`.
A reusable step performed inline in a proof or construction (a conversion between two forms of a definition, an auxiliary map) is extracted as its own API lemma or definition.
A PR created with AI assistance discloses that fact and the manner of use in its description.
A proof is kept as short as a reasonable reader can make it; a visibly compressible proof is golfed.
A change to a tool's observable output (message severity, format) is checked for downstream tooling that depends on it.
A proof that is a single lemma application with short arguments is written as one term rather than as a tactic block with `apply` and bullets.
A PR introducing a new concept, a non-obvious design choice or a change whose benefit is not self-evident explains its motivation and intended use in the description or module docstring.
A tactic's argument syntax reuses an existing syntax category (binders, `intro`/`rintro` patterns) rather than introducing a new parser for the same notion.

A PR is kept to one coherent unit; parts that can be reviewed separately (a file move, a preliminary refactor) or that need separate design discussion or further development are split into their own PRs.
A module docstring ends with `-/` immediately after its last line of text, with no blank line before it.
A lemma assumes a hypothesis, or ambient data such as a valuation, only when the statement needs it; an unnecessary assumption is dropped.
When a PR adds results to a file, the module docstring is updated to mention them.
An argument that appears only in the conclusion and in no hypothesis is explicit.
A `match` on an inductive type names every constructor it passes through unchanged rather than using a wildcard catch-all.
Anonymous functions are written with `↦`, not `=>`.
Arguments common to several consecutive declarations are declared once with `variable` rather than repeated in each signature.
A result whose converse also holds is stated as an iff.
A new file is imported in `Mathlib.lean` so that CI builds it.
A new file is a `module` with its content in an `@[expose] public section` unless a smaller public API is deliberately curated.
Plain `intro` is used when it handles the patterns; `rintro` is reserved for patterns `intro` cannot destructure.
In a mechanical cleanup, a hunk that makes the code longer or less readable is left out rather than applied for uniformity.
A term that already has the required type is supplied directly, not wrapped in a tactic block that merely produces it (`by exact e`, `by simpa using e`, `by infer_instance` for `inferInstance`).
Grouping delimiters the parser does not need — extra parentheses, braces around a tactic block, `<|` before a trailing `fun` — are omitted.
An instance that typeclass inference already finds is removed rather than redeclared (kept as an `example` at most).
A file-wide `set_option` (such as a linter threshold) is placed where the library's other files place the same option.
A function or lemma in the namespace of its argument's type is applied with dot notation (`x.f`, `h.foo`) rather than `T.f x`.

Spacing follows the style guide: a single space between tokens — after each comma, around infix operators and `:=`, between a name and its binders — a space inside structure-instance braces, and none before a comma, after a prefix operator or inside brackets.
The dedicated library lemma is used rather than an equivalent composite assembled from other lemmas.
A class or structure is given an alternative constructor that, under a common extra assumption, asks only for the fields that do not follow from it.
A `refine` whose term contains no placeholder, or an `apply` that leaves no goals, is written as `exact`.
A statement is written beta-reduced; an applied lambda `(fun x ↦ e) a` is replaced by its value.

A chain of compositions or transitivity steps (`Eq.trans`, `refine … ?_`) whose intermediate terms are implicit or recorded in comments is written as a `calc` or `trans` chain that states them in code.
A message that proposes replacement syntax follows the standard `Try this:` format.
A recurring combination of hypotheses about an object is bundled into a Prop-valued class that lemmas assume, rather than passing the data and hypotheses each time.
A declaration's statement continued onto a new line is indented by four spaces.
The components of a name follow the statement's structure: the head symbol of the left-hand side first, then its arguments in order, with projections and coercions (`coe_`, `toFoo_`) leading.
A lemma connecting two notions lives in the file of the more derived notion, so the more basic file does not import the more specialised one.
A declaration or file that is removed is given a deprecation alias or a redirecting stub, never silently deleted.
When a lemma name mentions another declaration, that declaration's name keeps its own camelCase spelling rather than being split into snake_case.
A deprecation whose replacement is not a drop-in substitute states in its message how to recover the old form.
Material whose topic or import requirements differ from a file's subject is placed in a new file, or in the existing file on its topic, rather than appended to that file.
A `set_option`, `omit` or `variable` binder change needed by particular declarations is scoped to them with `in` rather than applied to the rest of the file or section.
A backward-compatibility workaround option is re-checked against current master and removed once no longer necessary.
A proof does not chain normalising tactics (`simp`, `norm_num`, `ring_nf`) whose interaction produces a large fragile goal; it rewrites into a clean form and finishes with one call.
A hypothesis whose necessity is not evident is justified in the docstring or a comment, or by a reference.
An unreachable case is closed with an explicit contradiction (`False.elim`, `absurd`) rather than a tactic that closes the goal as a side effect.
The test suite of an additive (or otherwise dualised) tool mirrors every test of the original that has an analogue.
When an attribute or convention is applied systematically, the deliberate exceptions are documented in a comment.
A deprecated declaration is kept only as an alias or a one-line derivation from its replacement, not with its original proof.
The simp lemmas about one function, and the analogues of a lemma across the library, all orient towards the same normal form; a lemma is not oriented against its siblings.
Code or prose that fits within the 100-character limit is kept on one line rather than wrapped early.
A refactoring of meta-code preserves the existing behaviour in every case, including corner cases that do not currently arise.
A lemma that combines two independent operations is decomposed into a lemma for each operation, from which the combination follows.
A definition producing data is written as a term (pattern matching, direct construction), not built in tactic mode.
A PR whose content is unrelated to Mathlib (personal files, a test of scripts or automation) is closed; the repository is not a scratch space.
Meta-code that matches an expression against a known head constant uses `match_expr` or a Qq pattern rather than raw `mkApp`/`.const` constructor patterns.
An inequality step that follows by monotonicity or congruence is discharged by `gcongr` rather than by naming the specific monotonicity lemmas.

A lemma whose main hypothesis is a predicate `P x` takes that hypothesis as an explicit argument and is named in `P`'s namespace, so it is applied with dot notation, rather than being stated as an iff or in another namespace.
A safety check in meta-code is not bypassed by a flag for a special caller; the caller's context is adjusted (an instance locally removed) so that the check still runs.

A continuation block (tactic block, match-arm body, structure-instance fields, the continuation line of a bullet item in prose) is indented two spaces relative to its parent line, not further and not aligned to a delimiter.
Each tactic stands on its own line; several tactics are not joined with `;` on one line.
A PR that generalises or moves an existing declaration keeps its attributes (`@[simp]` and others) unchanged; an attribute change is made deliberately and separately.
An attribute on a declaration whose statement spans several lines is placed on its own line above the declaration keyword.
Commented-out code, leftover scaffolding comments and TODOs already carried out are removed before merging.
An instance obtained by inference after unfolding is supplied as `inferInstanceAs` with the unfolded type, not by `change`/`dsimp` followed by `infer_instance` in tactic mode.
A lemma stated as an equality of bundled maps (a composition equal to another map) is accompanied by its pointwise version applied to an element.
A new definition ships with the basic API lemmas that motivate it (closure under the standard operations, characterisations), not only the definition.
Two bundled maps that agree are related by an equation between the maps themselves, through the appropriate projection and tagged `@[simp]`, rather than only by a pointwise equation.
A variable is not named with a letter that carries an established meaning in the file's area (`ε` for a small real in analysis).
An equality lemma is stated in one orientation only; the reverse is obtained with `.symm` rather than stated as a second lemma.
A definition or proof that follows a source (a textbook, the Stacks project, a paper) cites that source in its docstring, so the convention adopted or the argument's origin is clear.
Side goals of a lemma application are supplied explicitly in a `refine` term rather than dispatched by `any_goals`/`try`/`<;>` combinator chains.
A new type or definition for a notion the library already names in another guise takes the established name rather than a fresh one.
A definition's docstring is a noun phrase naming the object defined, not a sentence describing what the function does.
Nested single-binder lambdas `fun a ↦ fun b ↦ e` are written as one lambda with several binders `fun a b ↦ e`.
A lemma or auxiliary definition that exposes the implementation of a definition and serves only to build its public API is marked `private`.
A definition, notation or instance is not introduced only to be unfolded by a `@[simp]` lemma; either it is the simp normal form or it is not added.

When the data at hand fits a structure's constructor, the structure is built directly from it rather than through an intermediate object and a conversion, and the intermediate is dropped if nothing else needs it.
A predicate or function on values of a type `T` is declared in `T`'s namespace so that it is written with dot notation (`s.IsDiscrete`).
A lemma whose formal statement obscures its meaning (filter language, an encoding) carries a docstring stating it in plain words.
A line break inside an expression comes after an infix operator (`→`, `∧`, `=`), not before it.
A step that contributes nothing (an unused `have`, a rewrite the closing step already covers, a check that a later call repeats) is removed.
A lemma that another lemma duplicates or that a general API lemma subsumes is deprecated in favour of that lemma rather than kept, or pointed at, alongside it.
A structure or subtype element used as a function is applied through its coercion (`x v`), not through the raw projection (`x.1 v`, `x.val v`).
A lemma that replaces one notion by another, rather than simplifying within one, is tagged `@[simp]` only when the target notion is the agreed normal form.
A structure of morphisms or data determined by its fields carries `@[ext]` globally, not only as a local attribute.
A non-obvious arrangement in a file (an unusual import, a deliberate omission) or a non-obvious choice within a proof is explained by a comment at the place it is made.
A docstring is written in complete sentences, each ending with a full stop.
Within a PR or a file, the same kind of step or the same notation is written the same way throughout (`have` or `haveI`, one spelling, one spacing), not in mixed forms.
A definition states its type explicitly rather than leaving it to be inferred from the body.
A simp lemma whose right-hand side is a `match` or `if` is replaced by one simp lemma per case, each with a concrete argument.
A monotonicity lemma concluding `f a ≤ f b` from `a ≤ b` is named `f_le_f`, without an `_of_le` suffix for the evident hypothesis.
A long proof inside a definition or instance is split off into a (private) auxiliary lemma rather than written inline, even if used once.
A citation points to the precise location in the work (chapter, section, tag), not only to the work.
A fix or improvement made to one of a family of analogous tools or declarations is applied to its siblings as well.
A `simp` that feeds another tactic is not hidden inside `simpa using by tac`; it is written as a visible `simp only [...]` followed by that tactic, or folded into the tactic's own lemma list.
A `conv` targets its subterm by pattern (`conv in`) rather than by a navigation path (`lhs; rhs; enter`).
A module docstring uses only the section headings the style guide prescribes; ad hoc headings are removed and their text merged into the prose.
The `Authors:` line of a file's header, and a PR's co-author credits, list every contributor.
A property that the PR's title or docstring ascribes to an object in the library's own terms (`Splits`, `IsCompact`) is stated as a lemma in that term, not left implicit in an equivalent formulation.
Within a statement or term-mode body spanning several lines, each line continuing a subexpression is indented two spaces beyond the line it continues, so indentation mirrors nesting.
A change of marginal benefit (cosmetic spacing in prose, minor docstring polish) is not made when reviewing it costs more than it gains.
A new or changed piece of meta-code (tactic, attribute, command, syntax) comes with tests in the test suite that exercise it.
A declaration's name is cased by its kind: a structure, inductive or `Type`/`Prop`-valued definition in UpperCamelCase, a function or term in lowerCamelCase, a theorem in snake_case.
An implicit argument that must be pinned is supplied directly (`@f a`, `(x := a)`, an explicit-argument variant `mk'`) rather than through a type ascription of the whole term.
A definition's docstring accounts for every component of its type — each non-obvious argument and each part of the result — not only the headline one.
A lemma concluding `f a ≤ f b` (or `<`) from `a ≤ b`, possibly with side conditions, is tagged `@[gcongr]`.
A term containing `?_` placeholders is passed to `refine`, not `apply`.
When code changes, the comment or docstring describing it is updated in the same change so that it stays accurate.
An automation call (`aesop`, `simp`, `grind`) is not replaced by explicit lemma names unless a benchmark shows it slow; such a change states its measured motivation.
A file all of whose declarations are deprecated is itself marked as a deprecated module.
When a definition has a preferred lemma for unfolding or using it, the definition's docstring points to that lemma.
Variables introduced by `induction` or `cases` are named through the structured `with | case x ih =>` syntax, not recovered afterwards with `rename_i`.
A lemma whose conclusion is a predicate `P x` is named `P.of_<hypothesis>` in `P`'s namespace, so that it is written `.of_h h` against the expected type.
A variant of an existing lemma is distinguished by a suffix naming what differs (`_of_<hypothesis>`), not by a prime.

A `by_cases` one of whose branches is impossible under the hypotheses, or whose branches do not use the case hypothesis, is replaced by the direct proof (a `have` of the fact that holds, or the one-arm proof).
A hypothesis that is a conjunction or existential whose components are always used separately is destructured when introduced (`obtain ⟨_, _⟩`), not projected with `.1`/`.2` at each use.
A definition's name, notation or a docstring's wording uses the standard mathematical term or convention for the notion, not one whose established meaning differs or a non-standard one.
A statement or use site does not need `@`, placeholder underscores or a type ascription to elaborate; a name or API that forces them is changed so that ordinary application suffices.
An `iff` lemma whose directions are useful on their own is accompanied by `alias ⟨_, _⟩` names for each direction, so each can be used with dot notation.
A lemma that is a direct instance of an existing general lemma, provable by applying it with no further work, is not added; the general lemma is used.
A lemma or instance states the strongest conclusion its proof gives (the tightest bound, the stronger filter, `Unique` over `Subsingleton`), not a weaker consequence of it.
A PR's title and description say concretely what the change is, and are kept current with it, so the git history is informative without the diff.
A note addressed to reviewers (an alternative considered, an open choice) is made as a PR comment, not left as a comment in the code.
An `iff` lemma puts the more complex or composite side on the left and the simpler side on the right, so that it reads and rewrites as a simplification.
A deprecation points to a live replacement, never to another deprecated declaration.
Where the library provides notation for a notion (`[[a, b]]` for `uIcc`), statements use the notation rather than the underlying name.

A function-valued definition, field or local `have` puts its binders or pattern-matching equations in its header (`f x y := e`, `f | pat => e`, `have h (x) (hx : p x) : … := …`), not in a `fun` after `:=` or introduced afterwards with `intro`.
A wrapper type is a one-field structure, whose constructor and projection are the conversions, rather than a `def` synonym with hand-made equivalences.
A definition generalised to a weaker setting (semiring for ring) is the mathematically right notion there, not a transliteration that happens to typecheck.
A declaration body (statement and proof) contains no blank line.
An instance whose name matters — because an attribute (`@[simps]`, `@[to_dual]`, `@[to_additive]`) derives names from it or because it is referenced — is named explicitly rather than left anonymous.
A namespace whose members are used repeatedly in a section is opened (`open Foo in`) rather than written out at each use.
A definition is unfolded by naming it in `simp`, `rw` or `unfold`, not by a `show _ = _ from rfl` or a `change` that restates its body.
A statement about a filter (`∀ᶠ`, `Tendsto`) is used through the filter API rather than unpacked into explicit sets and membership.
When a structure is built from an existing structure that supplies several of its fields, those fields are inherited with `__ := existing` rather than copied one by one.
A proof line that packs several non-trivial mathematical moves into one dense expression is split into separate steps, even if longer.
A name component is written in its unambiguous form (`VonNeumann`, `finset_sum`) when the short form could refer to something else.
A definition analogous to an existing library function (a sum, a fold, a map) takes its arguments in the same shape and order as that function.
A bound variable that the body does not use is written as `_`, not given a name.
A lemma that moves a cast through an operation or a literal is tagged `@[norm_cast]`.
A `simps` attribute is configured (`@[simps! apply]`) so that the generated lemma is stated at the level of application downstream uses need, not fully applied.
A definition obtained by reusing another across a definitional equality restates the fields whose types differ (`toFun`), so that generated lemmas mention the intended types.
A variable named after a Greek letter is written with the Unicode letter (`μ`, `φ`), not its transliteration (`mu`, `phi`).
A test of a tactic asserts the state it produces (`guard_target`, `guard_hyp`), not only that the tactic runs without error.
A type synonym introduced to carry instances different from the original type's is kept opaque to typeclass inference, not marked reducible for it.
Inside a tactic proof an instance hypothesis is introduced with `have`, not `haveI`; `haveI` is reserved for statements and term-mode where inlining is needed.
In a definition, the data it is built from is an explicit argument even when a hypothesis argument determines it, because a definition is applied to the data rather than to the proof.
A docstring that introduces a variable or a piece of notation says what the variable ranges over.
A definition or statement of the form `∀ x, x ∈ s → …` makes the bound variable strict-implicit (`∀ ⦃x⦄, x ∈ s → …`), so that it is inferred from the membership proof.
A name does not spell out instance hypotheses (`fully_faithful`, `preserves_mono`) that are not needed to distinguish it from another declaration.
An instance needed in several proofs of a section is registered once as a `local instance` rather than obtained by a `have` in each proof.
An exception in `noshake.json` is not added to keep an import the shake linter flags; the import is removed or its need fixed instead.
A purely stylistic change that the style guide does not prescribe is left to the author's discretion and is not imposed by a third party.
An attribute on a declaration tagged `to_additive` is passed through `to_additive (attr := …)` so that the additive version receives it too.
A definition takes a concrete bundled morphism type (`RingEquiv`) as its argument, not a `FooClass`-generic one; `FooClass` hypotheses are for lemmas.
A proof uses the most elementary tools that suffice, so that the result can be placed as early in the import hierarchy as possible.
A lemma's conclusion is stated in its simplest form (`1`, not `exp 0`), not in an expression that simplifies further.
A file does not pull in imports from a distant or heavier part of the library for a minor need; the dependency is avoided or the needed lemma stated in a lower file.
A new definition that is definitionally a known library object is connected to it by an explicit (possibly `rfl`) equivalence or lemma, so the connection is discoverable.
A structure field does not quantify over all types of a universe when a formulation over the carrier itself suffices.
A structure's axioms are chosen so that its morphisms are the natural maps; a laxer variant that makes maps awkward gets its own name (`Pre…`).
A small number of general lemmas are placed in the existing file where their subject lives (as `#find_home` suggests), not in a new file created for them.
When a lemma is generalised, its new hypothesis is a class that the original setting satisfies by an instance, so the special case still applies without extra work.
The general algebraic lemma is used rather than its type-specific copy (`zero_mul`, not `Nat.zero_mul`) when both apply.
A membership characterisation `mem_foo : x ∈ foo ↔ …` is named without an `_iff` suffix; the `↔` is implied by the `mem_` form.
A lemma about a type synonym is stated through the synonym's own API (its own `valuation`), not by applying the original structure across the definitional equality.
A definition written for kernel reduction or proof convenience that is slow to execute is paired with an efficient implementation via `@[csimp]`.
The dual of a lemma is generated by `to_dual`/`to_additive` rather than stated by hand and linked with `existing`.

A deprecated declaration whose replacement has a different signature (other explicit arguments or hypotheses) is kept with its original statement under `@[deprecated]`, not aliased to the replacement, so existing uses keep compiling.
A declaration's docstring points to closely related, overlapping or stronger declarations elsewhere in the library (`See also …`).
A notion made a class, which fixes one canonical instance per type, is also available as a plain structure when a type naturally carries several of them at once.

When a new simp lemma changes the simp normal form, existing lemmas stated in the old form are restated (or given a version) in the new form, rather than the simp lemma being excluded with `-lemma` at use sites.
A lemma with hypotheses that `simp` must discharge is tagged `@[simp]` only with justification that its side conditions are ones `simp` reliably proves.
A goal that a lighter, more targeted tactic (`simp`, `omega`, `lia`, `cutsat`, `positivity`) closes is closed by that tactic rather than by `grind`.
A PR description follows Mathlib's template and states only what reviewers need; boilerplate sections (test plan, implementation notes) are left out.
A name carries a prime only to distinguish a variant from an existing unprimed declaration; a prime with no unprimed counterpart is dropped.
A definition's docstring says what the object is (its defining formula or characterisation), not merely a restatement of its type.
Declarations are placed in the namespace where the library keeps the analogous results about the same objects (the class or structure they concern), not at the root or in an unrelated namespace.
A constructor or function that takes many data and proof arguments bundles them into a structure and takes one term of it, so that structure-instance syntax and code actions apply.
A new structure or definition is not introduced only to package the content of a single statement; that statement is written as a lemma (an iff with an existential) instead.
The two directions of an `iff` are taken with `.mp`/`.mpr`, not `.1`/`.2`.
A file's name and directory describe its actual content; a file whose content has drifted from its name is moved or renamed.
An eponymous adjective (Noetherian, Artinian, Hausdorff) is capitalised in prose and docstrings.
The most general version of a construction takes the plain name; a special case is the one that carries a distinguishing suffix.
Meta-code invokes another tactic through its `MetaM`/`TacticM` implementation function rather than by building syntax and calling `evalTactic`.
A PR does not add new uses of API that is being deprecated or refactored; it waits for, or builds on, the replacement.

A field of a specific, non-canonical instance is accessed as a projection of that instance term (`(inst).field x`), not through the class projection with the instance pinned (`C.field (self := inst) x`, `@C.field … inst x`).
A name uses the library's standard abbreviation for a word (`fun` for function, `hom`, `equiv`), not a different shortening.
A test case carries a comment saying what behaviour it checks, so that later edits do not defeat its purpose.
A docstring that points to another file refers to it by its file name, in the form the library uses elsewhere.
The docstring of a `TFAE` or otherwise indexed statement lists the items with numbers matching their indices, not bullets.
A PR title follows the commit convention: a type prefix (`feat`, `chore`, `fix`) with the area in parentheses, then a concise description.
A tactic proof opens with `by` at the end of the `:=` line, not at the start of the next line.
Projection lemmas of a definition (`_apply`, `_fst`, `_snd`) are generated with `@[simps]` rather than written by hand.
Lemmas about the components of an applied function are named with the projection as a suffix (`f_apply_fst`), following the `simps` naming, not with the projection first (`fst_f`).
A local term that carries data (a `Fintype` instance, a function) is introduced with `let`, not `have`, so that its value is not forgotten.
Lemmas assume the weakest class that supplies exactly what they use; when the needed combination of existing classes has no name, a class for it is introduced.
A PR that replaces proofs by heavier automation (`grind`, `simp_all`) reports its measured effect on compile time.

When a cleanup removes the last violation of a layering or dependency rule, the corresponding linter (directory dependency, forbidden import) is strengthened to forbid it, so the cleanup cannot regress.
A term-mode proof follows `:=` on the statement line only when the whole declaration fits on one line; otherwise `:=` ends the statement and the proof begins on the next line.
Rewriting or unfolding at default transparency (`erw`-style behaviour) is tracked as technical debt; new tooling or options that enable it are not added.
A goal that `rfl` closes only by unfolding definitions is instead proved by rewriting with the API lemmas stating those equalities, so the proof does not rely on definitional unfolding.
A definition that merely abbreviates a short expression in existing operations (`t + 1`) is not added; the expression is written directly.
A goal of the form `∀ᶠ x in l, p x` is proved with `filter_upwards [h₁, …] with x hx`, not by a manual `Eventually.mono`/`eventually_of_mem` application followed by `intro`.
A property needed only by some results (a size bound, non-degeneracy, coplanarity) is a hypothesis on those lemmas, not a field of a separate structure defined for the restricted case.

A function's non-obvious behaviour or presumed context (a mode it forces, an environment it assumes) is stated in its docstring, and reflected in its name where it matters, not only in an internal comment.
A tactic acts on the hypotheses it needs, named explicitly (`at h₁ h₂ ⊢`), not on the whole context with `at *`.
An instance that nothing refers to by name is left anonymous, taking the auto-generated name, rather than named by hand.
A tactic is chosen for the work it actually does: a `norm_num` or `simp` call whose only effect is rewriting with one lemma is written as `simp only [that lemma]` or `rw`.
Cast lemmas (`Int.cast_add`, `Int.cast_neg`, `Nat.cast_ofNat`) are not listed in a `simp only`; casts are normalised with `push_cast` or `norm_cast`.
A lemma that holds only under a restrictive hypothesis carries that hypothesis in its name (`_of_subsingleton`), so the name does not promise more than the statement.
A statement bundling two independently useful facts (an `IsGreatest`, a conjunction) is stated as one lemma per fact.
Notation that is standard in its area is declared `scoped` in the relevant namespace, so other files can open it, rather than `local` to one file.
An `example` does not live in a library file: a check of a tactic goes to the test suite, a fact worth keeping becomes a theorem, and the rest is removed.
An equation between composable morphisms in a category is tagged `@[reassoc]` (typically `@[reassoc (attr := simp)]`) so it also applies inside longer compositions.
A lemma's name follows the pattern of the sibling lemmas it sits beside (same suffixes, same elisions), not a scheme of its own.
A multi-line comment not attached to a declaration is written as a `/- … -/` block, not a run of `--` lines and not `/-- … -/`, which is reserved for docstrings.
Declaration names in comments and docstrings are enclosed in backticks so the documentation renders and links them.
A lemma's name states its conclusion first and its hypotheses after `_of_`, in that order.
A docstring says concretely what the declaration does or uses, not a vague gesture (`relevant information`, `some conditions`).
Declarations about one notion (a definition and its lemmas) are grouped together in a file, not scattered among unrelated sections.
